articles.title: 2026 Sydney Marathon: Addisu Gobena sets men's course record in victory; Peres Jepchirchir wins women's race
articles.summary: Gobena finished second in Sydney a year ago. He came out on top this time around.
articles.body:
A runner-up last year in the Sydney Marathon, Ethiopian Addisu Gobena won the event on Saturday, emerging from a field that featured the 2025 winner, fellow Ethiopian Hailemaryam Kiros, and the reigning world champion, Tanzania's Alphonce Simbu.

Gobena, 21, smashed Kiros' course record of 2:06:06 with a time of 2:04:42.

Although Simbu was taken down, the 2025 world champion on the women's side, Kenya's Peres Jepchirchir, wasn't defeated in Australia. The 32-year-old Jepchirchir, a 2021 Olympic gold medalist, finished just nine seconds shy of the course record, clocking in at 2:18:31.

In its second year as a World Marathon major — there are currently seven (the others are Tokyo, Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago and New York City) — the Sydney Marathon hosted around 40,000 expected runners who raced from North Sydney, across the Sydney Harbor Bridge and to the finish line, which was located in front of the city's iconic Opera House.

The Sydney Marathon marked the fourth event on this year's Marathon Major calendar. With a more demanding course than some of the majors, there was once again plenty of intrigue in Sydney. Last year, Kiros finished first among the men, while Sifan Hassan, a three-time Olympic gold medalist representing the Netherlands, took home the women's in 2:18:22. She didn't take part in Saturday's race, however.

This time around, Kenya's Priscah Cherono led all women at the 10-kilometer mark. The 46-year-old, who won the Los Angeles Marathon earlier this year after recently making a comeback from a five-year hiatus , was being chased by a collection of elites. That group included Jepchirchir, her compatriot.

Cherono was finally caught, about 30 kilometers in. Jepchirchir surged and so did Tanzania's Magdalena Shauri and Kenya's Irine Cheptai. Jepchirchir and Cheptai ultimately overtook Cherono, and Jepchirchir pulled ahead near the 35-kilometer mark.

In the end, no one reeled in Jepchirchir, who was stunningly close to topping Hassan's course record from a year ago.

As for the men's race, through 20 kilometers, it was on pace to shatter the course record. Humorously, two people dressed as Mario and Luigi were matching the speed of the lead runners for a good bit of time while on the sidelines.

Notably, Ethiopian Sisay Lemma dropped back from the top group as the race wore on. Lemma won Boston in 2024 but has struggled with injuries in recent years.

Through 40 kilometers, the men's pack was seven deep, with Kiros, Gobena and Simbu all contending.

Gobena made his move and wound up taking more than a minute off the previous course record Kiros had notched, holding off another Ethiopian, Chimdessa Debele, with a final push.

articles.title: Germany retain Hockey World Cup crown after Struthoff’s 44th-minute strike sinks Spain
articles.summary: Hockey News: Germany’s men’s hockey team were crowned world champions after beating Spain at Belfius Hockey Arena in Wavre, Belgium, on Sunday.They successfully de.
articles.body: Germany’s men’s hockey team were crowned world champions after beating Spain at Belfius Hockey Arena in Wavre, Belgium, on Sunday.They successfully defended their World Cup crown for the second time in history and became only the second team, after Pakistan, to win the title four times. Coached by André Henning, Germany had lost to Spain in the second round earlier in the tournament. But they came out on top when it mattered most, securing a 1-0 victory courtesy of Michel Struthoff’s goal in the 44th minute.Against the run of play, Germany went on the offensive and released Struthoff inside the semi-circle. He did brilliantly to guide the ball past Spanish goalkeeper Luis Calzado on the run.Struthoff had another opportunity to double Germany’s lead in the final quarter but could not keep his shot on target this time. It ultimately did not matter as Germany held on to lift the trophy.Speaking after the match, Germany captain Christopher Ruhr, who was named Player of the Match, was delighted to prove the doubters wrong.“I think everyone said, ‘Ah, the Germans this year? Nah, they won’t be there.’ Everyone focused on the other teams, but we showed what we’re capable of and played an amazing competition,” Ruhr told the broadcaster.“It was unbelievably tough. I think Spain played a hell of a tournament. We always struggle against Spain — they’re a tough side, and they played a really good game today. We had the lucky end.”Spain indeed dominated large parts of the game, recording nine shots on goal, 24 circle entries and four penalty corners. But Germany defended resolutely to deny Spain their maiden World Cup title.But their victory would not have been possible without the heroic efforts of goalkeeper Jean-Paul Danneberg. He made several superb saves throughout the match, including a brilliant stop with his left hand to deny Borja Lacalle from the left. His presence also forced the Spaniards to go wide during their penalty corners and that made a huge difference.Germany, however, did not look at their best in the opening stages. Their crosses often lacked precision, while heavy touches repeatedly disrupted their attacking moves and allowed Spain to threaten. In the end, however, the Germans did just enough to secure the win and retain their world title.It was also heartbreak for Spain coach Max Caldas, who had previously lost a World Cup final in 2018 while coaching Netherlands. The Dutch side had gone down to Belgium in a shootout at Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar.Meanwhile, there was further heartbreak for Netherlands, who finished without a World Cup medal for the first time since 2006. They lost 1-2 to Argentina in the bronze-medal match earlier on Sunday.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Corrida da Serra fecha o calendários de provas 2026 no Paraná | G1
articles.standfirst: Percursos de até 10 km cortam a Mata Atlântica em Morretes, cidade histórica do litoral do Paraná, em 13 de dezembro.
articles.summary: Percursos de até 10 km cortam a Mata Atlântica em Morretes, cidade histórica do litoral do Paraná, em 13 de dezembro.
articles.body:
Cercada pela Mata Atlântica e cortada pelo Rio Nhundiaquara, Morretes, cidade histórica do litoral do Paraná, é o tipo de lugar em que o tempo parece passar mais devagar, entre casarões coloniais e o cheiro de barreado saindo das panelas de barro. Mas em dezembro a cidade muda de ritmo. A Corrida da Serra Verde Express chega à sua 2ª edição no dia 13 de dezembro de 2026, com largada marcada para às 6h30, reunindo esportistas de diferentes níveis em trechos que atravessam alguns dos cenários mais bonitos do litoral paranaense. A expectativa da organização, a Serra Verde Express, é reunir mais de 1.000 participantes, quase o dobro do público que compareceu à estreia do evento, em 2025.

"A primeira edição superou todas as expectativas. Reunimos mais de 600 atletas e movimentamos a cidade com cerca de 50 pessoas envolvidas na organização. O que mais nos surpreendeu foi perceber que os participantes começaram a enxergar Morretes com outros olhos, como um destino para atividade física, lazer, ecoturismo e descanso. A corrida está se tornando uma porta de entrada para o turismo na região" , afirma Adonai Arruda Filho, diretor-geral da Serra Verde Express, empresa que opera o passeio de trem pela Serra do Mar Paranaense e organiza a prova.

Onde fica Morretes, a cidade que virou point de corrida no litoral do Paraná

Morretes fica no litoral do estado do Paraná, a cerca de 70 km de Curitiba, a capital paranaense, um trajeto que pode ser feito em aproximadamente uma hora de carro ou em um dos passeios de trem que cortam a Serra do Mar. A cidade também está a cerca de 40 km de Paranaguá e a 15 km de Antonina, dois outros municípios turísticos do litoral do estado.

Fundada em 1733, depois da descoberta de ouro na região, Morretes tem hoje cerca de 15 mil habitantes e mantém um dos conjuntos arquitetônicos coloniais mais preservados do sul do país. Entre os principais pontos históricos estão a Igreja Matriz de Nossa Senhora do Porto, do século 19, a Igreja de São Benedito e a ponte metálica sobre o Rio Nhundiaquara, curso d'água que corta o centro histórico e que já foi uma das principais vias de escoamento da erva-mate produzida na região.

Além da paisagem, a cidade também é conhecida no Brasil inteiro pelo barreado, prato típico do litoral paranaense preparado com carne bovina cozida lentamente, por horas, em panela de barro, temperada e servida com arroz branco, banana e farinha de mandioca. É justamente essa combinação de história, gastronomia e natureza preservada que tem atraído cada vez mais visitantes para o município, e que agora ganha um motivo a mais para levar gente à cidade: a corrida.

Alguns motivos que explicam por que Morretes vem se consolidando como destino:

Está a menos de duas horas de Curitiba, o que facilita passeios de um dia ou fins de semana mais longos

Reúne casario colonial preservado, rio, montanha e Mata Atlântica em um raio de poucos quilômetros

É ponto de chegada do histórico passeio de trem operado pela Serra Verde Express, considerado um dos trajetos ferroviários mais bonitos do país, com 70 km de extensão entre Curitiba e Morretes, 13 túneis e 41 pontes

Tem estrutura de pousadas, restaurantes e comércio local voltada ao turista

Está próxima de outros destinos do litoral, como Antonina e a Ilha do Mel

Percursos para todos os níveis: caminhada, 6 km e 10 km

A largada da 2ª Corrida da Serra Verde Express acontece no Coreto Jeff Petersen, na Praça dos Imigrantes, na Rua General Carneiro esquina com a Rua Coronel Rômulo José Pereira, no centro histórico de Morretes.

A prova tem duração máxima de duas horas. Quem não concluir o percurso dentro desse tempo é convidado a se retirar. Segundo as normas da Confederação Brasileira de Atletismo (CBAT), a idade mínima para participar das provas de 6 km e 10 km é de 16 anos. Os atletas devem chegar ao local de largada com pelo menos meia hora de antecedência, quando são passadas as últimas orientações da organização.

O trajeto da Corrida da Serra Verde Express leva os participantes por paisagens que só é possível ver de perto correndo ou caminhando a pé, com a Serra do Mar como pano de fundo e trechos que revelam a Mata Atlântica preservada da região, de um ângulo que nenhum outro meio de transporte oferece.

"Correr por Morretes é também descobrir recantos da Mata Atlântica, sentir o ritmo da cidade histórica e entender por que o litoral do Paraná está cada vez mais no radar de quem busca qualidade de vida e contato com a natureza" , garante Arruda Filho.

Não é a primeira vez que a Serra Verde Express aposta na conexão entre esporte, turismo e meio ambiente. A empresa já é conhecida pelo passeio de trem que liga Curitiba a Morretes cortando a Serra do Mar, e a corrida nasceu como uma forma de aproximar ainda mais o público desse cenário, agora em um ritmo diferente: o dos próprios pés.

Um dos objetivos da organização para esta edição é ampliar o público que participa do evento, para além dos corredores mais experientes. Por isso, o calendário de provas foi desenhado para incluir desde quem está começando na atividade física até quem já disputa corridas de rua com regularidade.

Caminhada de 3 km: ideal para famílias, iniciantes e quem quer apenas vivenciar o clima do evento

Corrida de 6 km: primeiro passo para quem já pratica corrida e quer encarar uma prova mais desafiadora

Corrida de 10 km: para atletas que já têm rotina de treino e buscam performance

A ideia é que cada participante encontre seu próprio ritmo dentro da programação, em uma celebração conjunta do esporte, da saúde e do bem-estar, sem deixar de lado o principal atrativo do evento, que é o cenário natural de Morretes.

Como funcionam as inscrições e os valores

As inscrições para a 2ª Corrida da Serra Verde Express estão abertas e organizadas em lotes, com valores que aumentam conforme as vagas vão sendo preenchidas:

Lote promocional (1º lote): de 12 de agosto a 30 de setembro de 2026, ou até acabarem as vagas, por R$ 135,00

2º lote: a partir do encerramento do 1º lote até 1º de dezembro de 2026, ou até acabarem as vagas, por R$ 155,00

O valor da inscrição inclui kit do atleta, com camiseta, sacochila, brindes dos apoiadores, número de peito, chip eletrônico de cronometragem, medalha de participação e hidratação durante o percurso. As inscrições podem ser encerradas a qualquer momento, assim que a organização atingir o limite técnico de vagas estabelecido para a prova, então quem já decidiu participar tem a recomendação de garantir a inscrição com antecedência.

Premiação: viagens, hospedagens e passeio de trem para os vencedores

A premiação é um dos destaques da Corrida da Serra Verde Express, e reforça justamente a ligação do evento com o turismo regional. "Na edição passada, premiamos os vencedores com experiências de viagem e hospedagem, porque acreditamos que o prêmio tem que estar conectado com o DNA da Serra Verde Express, que é o turismo. Este ano vamos surpreender ainda mais. Mas o mais importante é participar e fazer parte de um evento que cresce a cada ano" , reforça Adonai.

Corrida de 10 km (geral masculino e feminino)

1º lugar: viagem para João Pessoa (PB), com passagem aérea e hospedagem, durante o período da Maratona de João Pessoa, entre 15 e 19 de abril de 2027, com patrocínio da BWT Operadora. A premiação não inclui a inscrição na maratona: o atleta tem direito a transporte aéreo e hospedagem, conforme regras do patrocinador

Todos os atletas que concluírem a prova, em qualquer uma das modalidades, recebem medalha de participação. Além da premiação em viagens, também serão entregues troféus:

As faixas etárias consideradas são de 16 a 29 anos, de 30 a 39 anos, de 40 a 49 anos, de 50 a 59 anos, de 60 a 69 anos e acima de 70 anos, sempre levando em conta o ano de nascimento que o atleta completa até 31 de dezembro de 2026. A premiação acontece após a chegada de todos os participantes e não é entregue a representantes do atleta ausente, nem em outra oportunidade que não seja a cerimônia oficial.

articles.title: Why so many black Britons still don't swim
articles.summary: For decades, swimming ability has been lower in the black community. Our writer asks why.
articles.body:
As I push through the doors, the smell of chlorine hits me. Instantly, I feel sick, and I remember why I don't go swimming. I'm getting ready for my first swimming lesson in over 10 years, trying to convince myself it won't be so bad.

I glance around the pool; I'm surrounded by other black women learning to swim, all at different levels. Some are confidently swimming lengths; others, like me, are learning how to feel at home in the water.

I'm learning to breathe properly, dunk my head under and let the water carry me, rather than fight against it. There are so many things to remember.

At the age of 27, I'm still unable to swim - and I'm far from alone.

Swimming ability is not spread evenly across the population; figures compiled by Swim England, swimming's governing body, based on a survey of 4,500 people suggest poorer people, for example, are much less likely to be able to swim, as well as Muslims, people of South Asian descent and children known to social care.

As a black woman, it's the figures for the black community that always jump out to me. Swim England's figures suggest that 67% of black women and 44% of black men in England cannot swim 25 metres unaided - far higher than the national average, and far higher than the numbers for white people (17% of white women and 12% of white men cannot swim 25 metres). Behind those figures, published in 2022, are very different stories.

Over Britain's record-breaking hot summer, we've seen a number of tragic deaths in lakes, rivers, and at sea, all of which will contribute to the UK's annual total of drownings. There's no official data yet for 2026, but in previous years we've seen black children and adults over-represented in the drowning figures (along with those other groups mentioned above).

I see this as a stark reminder: learn to swim. All children in the UK are supposed to leave primary school able to swim. But just why are there so many black people, like me, who can't? It's a trend that's existed for decades, but one that has never been fully explained.

That was the conclusion of the University of Portsmouth, the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) and the Black Swimming Association (BSA) in 2023; together, they set out to test one of the most persistent myths surrounding black people and swimming: that black people have denser bones than white people, which makes it harder to float.

It's an idea with a long history. European accounts dating back to the 15th Century recorded that many west Africans were highly skilled swimmers and divers. But racial exclusion from pools in some countries, like the United States, helped to create the idea that black people were poor swimmers. In 1974, only a few years after the end of segregation in the US, an article by two white doctors in a respected US medical journal asked: "Can Blacks Float?". They concluded that black people were simply less buoyant than white people.

In fact, the Portsmouth study found that bone density could not predict whether someone could float. Of the 101 participants in the study, 89 floated unassisted for two minutes.

The UK did not have the same system of formal segregation as the US in the 20th Century. But Alice Dearing, a former Olympic swimmer and co-founder of the BSA, thinks that the US's history might have reverberated in parts of British culture too. Some black people have "ingrained within themselves to think that they can't swim", she says.

For Dearing, this is not just history. At 17, she says a coach used a racial slur about her to another swimmer. She later complained to her swimming club and school but ultimately decided not to take the matter further. "Why am I being victimised for swimming and for being black? It just didn't make sense," she says.

Experiences like these can shape how black people see themselves in the water. Heather Massey, a physiology professor at the University of Portsmouth who was involved in the floating study, says it's important to challenge those myths.

"If people believe they can't float, then they may be dismissing something that could eventually save their life," she says. "We need to make sure that we get the right information out there."

For most British children, swimming starts with their family. If parents swim, children grow up seeing the water as something familiar.

But if parents have not learned to swim - as is the case in some black families - then children are less likely to start swimming lessons at a young age.

I come from a family of non-swimmers: I'm one of five siblings and none of us can swim, neither can my parents. We still enjoyed days at the beach, but that usually meant walking along the coast or paddling in the shallows. Rarely did we go much deeper than knee height.

It's a pattern seen by Nathaniel Cole, co-founder of Swim Dem Crew, a swimming group encouraging more people of colour to get into the water. He remembers coaching children whose parents could not swim, and encouraging them to get into the pool with their children after lessons.

"But then the parents would be like, 'Well, I can't swim'," he says.

Cole says having parents who cannot swim can make the water seem dangerous. "Swimming underwater is something to be avoided. You don't go in there, there's danger. And unfortunately that's driven from parents that can't swim."

Dearing's experience was different. Her mother grew up swimming in the ocean in Accra, Ghana. "When she came over to the UK, she was going to make sure all of her children knew how to swim," she says.

Swimming was passed down in Dearing's family. In mine, it wasn't.

For those who never learnt as children, Cole says starting later can feel particularly exposing. "To be a beginner swimmer, you are humbled by the water," he says. "You have to be very vulnerable."

The barriers to swimming start long before you reach the water.

For Kevin Hylton, emeritus professor of equality and diversity in sport at Leeds Beckett University, that started with his childhood. "I grew up in a working-class Caribbean family where swimming wasn't a thing that was done," he says. "We had almost zero leisure as a family together. It was done through school."

His three children had a very different experience. By then, he and his partner had more disposable income and lived closer to swimming facilities. He says the difference, in his case, was not ethnicity. "It's because of class. And also because of location and the proximity to swimming facilities," he says.

That gap is reflected in the figures. Sport England figures said that 47% of children and young people in the most deprived areas could swim 25 metres, compared with 69% in the least deprived areas.

Access to pools can make that gap harder to close. More than 500 public swimming pools have closed across the UK since 2010, with almost half closing since 2020, according to Swim England and ukactive, the trade body for gyms and leisure centres. The charity classes one-fifth of local authorities as "water deprived", meaning they don't have enough swimming pool space to match their population.

But even when you take class into account, there's still a particular problem among black people. In 2022 Swim England also looked specifically at those in the most deprived neighbourhoods. On average, 73% of adults living in those poorer neighbourhoods could swim 25 metres; but for black adults in those neighbourhoods, it was just 38%.

And there are other thorny cultural factors too. In a 2023 survey by the BSA of more than 1,400 people, 33% of black British respondents named issues around their hair as a barrier to getting in the pool. The BSA wrote that "traditional aquatic headwear", like swimming caps, "doesn't cater to children with longer, thicker afro hair, nor does it cater to traditionally Black hairstyles including braids, dreadlocks and twists with extensions".

Back at my swimming class, I'm still struggling to hold down my fear.

I'm floating, first on my front and then on my back. I'm doing things I never thought I'd be able to do. And somehow, I'm enjoying myself.

My fear started in primary school when I had compulsory swimming lessons. I would arrive armed with what I liked to call my anti-drowning armour: armbands, floats, goggles, and a swimming hat.

But it still wasn't enough to make me feel safe. There were dozens of children in the pool, all at various levels, and I remember feeling overwhelmed rather than taught. Swimming became something I associated with fear.

"See, you can do it, you're floating," my instructor, Omie Dale, tells me proudly.

Swimming is different from other sports; not learning the skill can have consequences far beyond missing out on exercise.

England's National Child Mortality Database found that black children were over three times more at risk of drowning as white children between 2019 and 2025. Putting ethnicity aside, risk was also more than twice as high for children living in the most deprived areas compared with the least deprived.

And Hylton points out another startling figure: 71% of children who drown (of any race) had been known to social care at some point in their lives, according to the Royal Life Saving Society UK (RLSS UK).

Hylton calls for more research into why these children are so much more likely to drown.

Standing at the edge of the pool, I wondered how different things might have been if I'd kept learning after school.

Dale says many of her students have also not had a lesson since primary school, leaving years to pass before they get another chance to build confidence.

Despite the fact that swimming is part of the national curriculum in England and Northern Ireland, financial pressures are making it tough; even just the cost of paying for a coach to a swimming pool is too much for some schools.

Dale believes getting black children into the water early, and giving them the chance to keep returning, can help. "We run free lessons and we get so many young people who are natural swimmers and just love the water. If we hadn't been there at that stage, they could have grown up thinking they can't swim."

Seeing people like yourself in the water can make a difference. But at the highest levels of swimming, black representation remains low.

In 2019, the BBC found that of the 73,000 competitive swimmers registered with Swim England, just 668 - less than 1% - identified as black or mixed race. (About 4% of England's population is black).

In 2020, Dearing became the first black British woman to represent Team GB in swimming at an Olympic Games, competing in Tokyo. Her achievement matters beyond the pool. Sport England research found that a lack of visible role models can reinforce negative stereotypes about the abilities of people from ethnically diverse backgrounds.

"No one wants to be the… only black person in the pool," says Cole.

When I got out of the pool after my lesson, I felt something I hadn't expected: I wanted to get back in. For years, I had accepted being unable to swim. It was easier to avoid the water than to confront something that had frightened me since childhood.

I'm still a long way from being a confident swimmer, but already the world feels a little more open to me: the sea, rivers and lakes; kayaking and paddleboarding.

Dale describes swimming as a "gateway", saying that once you learn, "it opens a whole new world".

At 27, I am not a swimmer. But I am ready to learn.

articles.title: Germany beat Spain 1-0, retain Hockey World Cup crown
articles.summary: Hockey News: Germany’s men’s hockey team were crowned world champions after beating Spain at Belfius Hockey Arena in Wavre, Belgium, on Sunday.They successfully de.
articles.body: Germany’s men’s hockey team were crowned world champions after beating Spain at Belfius Hockey Arena in Wavre, Belgium, on Sunday.They successfully defended their World Cup crown for the second time in history and became only the second team, after Pakistan, to win the title four times. Coached by André Henning, Germany had lost to Spain in the second round earlier in the tournament. But they came out on top when it mattered most, securing a 1-0 victory courtesy of Michel Struthoff’s goal in the 44th minute.Against the run of play, Germany went on the offensive and released Struthoff inside the semi-circle. He did brilliantly to guide the ball past Spanish goalkeeper Luis Calzado on the run.Struthoff had another opportunity to double Germany’s lead in the final quarter but could not keep his shot on target this time. It ultimately did not matter as Germany held on to lift the trophy.Speaking after the match, Germany captain Christopher Ruhr, who was named Player of the Match, was delighted to prove the doubters wrong.“I think everyone said, ‘Ah, the Germans this year? Nah, they won’t be there.’ Everyone focused on the other teams, but we showed what we’re capable of and played an amazing competition,” Ruhr told the broadcaster.“It was unbelievably tough. I think Spain played a hell of a tournament. We always struggle against Spain — they’re a tough side, and they played a really good game today. We had the lucky end.”Spain dominated large parts of the game, recording nine shots on goal, 24 circle entries and four penalty corners. But Germany defended resolutely to deny Spain their maiden World Cup title.But their victory would not have been possible without the heroic efforts of goalkeeper Jean-Paul Danneberg. He made several superb saves throughout the match, including a brilliant stop with his left hand to deny Borja Lacalle from the left. His presence also forced the Spaniards to go wide during their penalty corners and made a huge difference.Germany, however, did not look at their best in the opening stages. Their crosses often lacked precision, while heavy touches repeatedly disrupted their attacking moves and allowed Spain to threaten. In the end, however, the Germans did just enough to secure the win and retain their world title.It was also heartbreak for Spain coach Max Caldas, who had previously lost a World Cup final in 2018 while coaching Netherlands. The Dutch side had gone down to Belgium in a shootout at Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar.Meanwhile, there was further heartbreak for Netherlands, who finished without a World Cup medal for the first time since 2006. They lost 1-2 to Argentina in the bronze-medal match earlier on Sunday.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Lindsey Vonn Set for Another Surgery on Leg Injury Suffered in Crash at 2026 Olympics
articles.summary: After a pair of devastating crashes earlier this year that left her with a torn ACL and a severely broken leg, Lindsey Vonn is still facing a long road to being fully recovered.
articles.body:
After a pair of devastating crashes earlier this year that left her with a torn ACL and a severely broken leg, Lindsey Vonn is still facing a long road to being fully recovered.

"I feel good, I'm getting better. I still have another surgery, so I'm trying to get as strong as possible," Vonn told TNT Sports in an interview at the US Open on Sunday (h/t Zack Pierce of The Athletic). "And once I get my ACL, then I'll have another long road ahead of me. But for now, I feel great, and I'm very thankful for that."

After qualifying for her fifth Olympic appearance in December, Vonn tore her ACL in a crash in a World Cup race in Crans-Montana, Switzerland, on Jan. 30, the final downhill before the Olympics began a week later. The American Alpine skiing star still opted to compete through the injury at the Milan Cortina Games, but she suffered another violent crash just 13 seconds into her first run. She was airlifted off the course and underwent multiple surgeries to repair a "complex tibia fracture" and save her leg from amputation.

The 41-year-old said that her surgery later this year will address her ACL, which still hasn't been repaired.

"I'm hoping that I can have the next surgery in November, but it'll be in the winter sometime, and then it'll be another nine months until I'm fully recovered from that, so I can't really look beyond that," she said. "I don't really know what the future holds, but like I said, I'm just thankful for where I am right now."

A four-time World Cup champion and 2010 Olympic gold medalist, Vonn has already enjoyed a legendary career, so she will focus on her recovery before making a decision on her future in the sport.

articles.title: Alba Sánchez: del infierno al oro en los Juegos Mediterráneos en Taranto
articles.standfirst: La halterófila española pisa el primer peldaño del podio tras unos meses complicados por una lesión. España suma más medallas en halterofilia, atletismo y triatlón.
articles.summary: La halterófila española pisa el primer peldaño del podio tras unos meses complicados por una lesión. Su medalla se suma a las otras XX ganadas por la delegación española esta jornada
articles.body: La halterofilia brindó dos medallas más a la delegación española en los Juegos Mediterráneos de Taranto (Italia). Alba Sánchez (-53 kg) se colgó el oro en dos tiempos al levantar 105 kilos en su tercer intento, nueva plusmarca nacional, tras haber logrado antes alzar 100 y 103. En arrancada se quedó a las puertas del podio con 81 kilos levantados, los mismos que la italiana Celine Ludovica Delia, pero está con dos intentos válidos por solo uno de la española. Los 186 kg en el total olímpico dieron también a Alba Sánchez otro récord de España. Sánchez, sobrina de Estefanía Juan, doble campeona de Europa en -48 kilos en su etapa en activo, no pudo contener la emoción cuando comprobó que el oro era suyo. "Estoy en schok, vengo de una lesión, de blanquearme en el Europeo y cuatro meses de no poder entrenar, de un auténtico infierno... Y de repente sacar el oro aquí es brutal", comentaba Alba Sánchez en declaraciones a las redes sociales de la Federación Española de Halterofilia. María Olalla (-61 kg) fue bronce en arrancada. Levantó 90 kg en su primer intento. Luego falló en los dos restantes sobre 95. En dos tiempos, subió un peldaño más en el podio. Se colgó la plata con 112 kg en su primer levantamiento. La italiana Martina Chiacchio fue oro con 120. El atletismo se sumó también a la fiesta de medallas con cuatro platas. En la segunda jornada de competición, los 800 metros brindaron dos segundos puestos en el podio a la delegación española. Lorea Ibarzabal logró la primera tras correr en 2:00.07. El oro fue para la croata Nina Vukovic (1:59.63). A continuación fue el turno de la prueba masculina. David Barroso, cuarto en el 800 del Europeo de Birmingham, acabó también segundo (1:46.35), por detrás del argelino Djamel Sedjati (1:46.00). Diego Casas también se colgó la plata en el lanzamiento de disco. Llegó a los 65,62 metros por los 68,70 del esloveno Kristjan Ceh. Carmen Rosales también logró esta misma medalla en longitud con 6,50 en su cuarto salto. No pudo superar los 6,59 de Filippa Fotopoulou que logró la chipriota en su primer contacto con la prueba. El triatlón también sumó una plata más al medallero. El equipo español, formado por Alejandra Seguí, Eduardo Blanco, Natalia Castro yJarno Pousada, fue segundo en el relevo mixto con un tiempo de 1:21:06 por detrás del combinado italiano (1:19:44). Es la segunda medalla del trialtón en estos Juegos tras el bronce de Edu Blanco. En gimnasia artística, Nicolau Mir, Thierno Diallo, Ignacio Yockers, Sergio Kovacs y Daniel Carrión lograron el bronce para el equipo masculino. Llegaron a los 234,400 puntos por los 238,400 de Turquía (oro) y los 237,000 de Italia (plata).

articles.title: Museu dedicado aos 'salsichinhas' reúne mais de 30 mil objetos | G1
articles.standfirst: Acervo tem papel higiênico, talheres e até bancos com a imagem da raça. Museu também recebe cães e oferece passeio por pontos de Regensburg ligados aos salsichinhas.
articles.summary: Acervo tem papel higiênico, talheres e até bancos com a imagem da raça. Museu também recebe cães e oferece passeio por pontos de Regensburg ligados aos salsichinhas.
articles.body:
Em uma cidade da Alemanha com mais de 2 mil anos de história, um museu tem um personagem inusitado como protagonista: o cachorro-salsicha, conhecido oficialmente como Dachshund.

O Museu do Dachshund fica em Regensburg, às margens do rio Danúbio, e reúne mais de 30 mil objetos relacionados à raça. No acervo, há de tudo: papel higiênico, talheres, abridores de vinho, saleiros e até bancos.

Também não faltam representações dos cães em madeira, cerâmica, vidro e pelúcia. E há salsichinhas de verdade circulando pelo espaço.

A Cocolina, por exemplo, visitou o museu acompanhada da família colombiana. Para a turista Maria Camila Matta, a quantidade de objetos relacionados à raça impressiona.

"Tem Cocolinas por todo lado. É lindo. Achei muito legal conhecer toda essa relação com a realeza e descobrir quantos monarcas tiveram teckels. Também fiquei surpreso ao saber que o Picasso tinha um. Eu não fazia ideia de que essa raça era tão famosa no mundo todo", contou.

Cão salsicha homenageado em museu da Alemanha — Foto: Dackelmuseum

O espaço recebe cerca de 35 mil visitantes humanos por ano. Com a presença dos cães, o movimento é ainda maior.

Além da exposição, o museu oferece um passeio pela cidade de Regensburg com paradas em locais que fazem referência aos cachorros.

Um dos fundadores, Oliver Storz, disse que a coleção começou muito antes da abertura do museu, em 2018. Foram mais de 20 anos reunindo objetos relacionados ao Dachshund.

"Recebemos muitas doações de todas as partes do mundo. No ano passado, uma senhora faleceu nos Estados Unidos e deixou em seu testamento que toda a sua coleção, com cerca de 800 peças, fosse doada ao Museu do Dachshund", disse.

Peças em exposição em museu voltado para cães salsichas — Foto: Deckelmuseum

Em 2024, o museu entrou para o Guinness World Records depois de reunir quase 900 Dachshunds em um desfile pelas ruas de Regensburg.

O evento, porém, também provocou críticas de entidades de proteção animal, que são contrárias à reprodução de cães com características consideradas extremas.

Na Alemanha, uma lei restringe a reprodução de animais que tenham características físicas capazes de provocar dor ou sofrimento. A discussão também alcança alguns tipos de Dachshund.

A raça foi desenvolvida na Alemanha a partir do século 15 para ajudar na caça de texugos. O corpo comprido e as pernas curtas facilitavam a entrada dos cães em tocas subterrâneas.

Com o passar do tempo, os Dachshunds deixaram de ser apenas cães de caça e se transformaram em um dos símbolos mais conhecidos da Alemanha.

A relação com a cultura do país chegou até aos Jogos Olímpicos de Munique, em 1972. Na ocasião, o mascote oficial foi Waldi, um Dachshund colorido.

Exposição com 'salsichas' na Alemanha — Foto: Dackelmuseum

Acervo tem papel higiênico, talheres e até bancos com a imagem da raça. Museu também recebe cães e oferece passeio por pontos de Regensburg ligados aos salsichinhas.

articles.title: Breaker Raygun on processing what happened at Paris 2024 Olympics
articles.summary: Australian Olympic breakdancer Rachael Gunn - known as Raygun - tells BBC Sport about the aftermath of her extraordinary experience at the 2024 Olympics.
articles.body:
Just hours before representing Australia at the Paris 2024 opening ceremony, Rachael Gunn had a panic attack in the middle of the Olympic village.

Thrust into an environment full of experienced athletes, it dawned on Gunn, whose professional background is as a university lecturer, what she had got herself into.

Known as Raygun when competing, she was about to take part in the breakdancing event - or breaking - which was making its Olympic debut.

"I felt like an imposter," said the 38-year-old breaker, during a new Netflix documentary about her experience at the Games.

She describes how she reacted when she saw someone she recognised from the Olympic team.

"I just could not stop crying... I had a panic attack. 'What am I doing? What have I done? Should I be doing this?'" she said.

Just a few hours later, she was sailing down the River Seine alongside the rest of the Australian cohort, waving to onlookers.

Less than a fortnight after that, her Olympic journey was over. Gunn failed to win any of her three round-robin battles at the Games, but walked away pleased with how she had acquitted herself.

"Finishing my last round, the world champion Nicka [Dominika Banevic] gave me props for my moves, the MC celebrated my stuff and the vibe was just generally good," Gunn told BBC Sport.

What she hadn't anticipated was that one of her performances, in which she debuted some unconventional moves including a sprinkler and a kangaroo hop, had gone viral.

There were memes. There was a sketch on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. Adele referenced the performance in one of her concerts. Chris Hemsworth defended Gunn in an interview with Jimmy Kimmel. At one point in August 2024, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese even felt moved to speak out, praising Gunn for having "a crack".

"It was pretty wild the way I became a topic of conversation in spaces I never thought I would be," said Gunn.

Alongside the teasing, there were more sinister forces brewing, including conspiracy theories about nepotism - for instance that Gunn's husband and trainer, Samuel Free, had been on the selection committee when she qualified to represent her country at the Games, when he hadn't been.

"It was really tough when mine and Sammy's credibility, ethics and motivations were being called into question," Gunn said.

"You could just spend 30 seconds researching and find plenty of sources to debunk these conspiracies, but that's not how people use the internet anymore."

That new-found scrutiny took a toll on Gunn's mental health.

"I felt like my whole life was just kind of crumbling before me.. .and I was just trying to get through the day," she says in the documentary.

In the process of making a film about that time, however, she feels that she's been able to regain some agency.

"It's taken a long time for me to process what happened," Gunn told BBC Sport.

"It's really exciting for me to finally have a voice again."

A new Olympic sport and a creative gamble

After it was announced that breaking would be included at Paris 2024, Gunn qualified to represent her country via the Oceania Breaking Championships in Sydney in 2023.

"I've never participated in anything of such high stakes before. It was all international judges, but I was relieved and excited when I qualified. And then the next whirlwind happened," she said.

Quickly, she realised that she would have to start living like an athlete.

Gunn gained a scholarship at the New South Wales Institute of Sport in February 2024, which allowed her to begin a strength and conditioning programme.

"That was great, but also overwhelming because I was training with people who had been doing that stuff since they were kids," she said.

In the midst of her training, the documentary reveals that Gunn's mother suffered three brain aneurisms. Gunn herself began a course of anti-depressants to help with feelings of anxiety.

The film portrays how it began to dawn on her what she had taken on when she entered competitions in the run up to the Games.

"That's when it first starting occurring to me that I was going to be going up against world champs and people who had been winning competitions on big stages for years and years, but I was still going to go out there and do my best," she says in the documentary.

In that context, Gunn decided to play to her own strengths with a creative gamble, developing a routine that paid cheeky homage to her Australian roots.

"I was aware that I was never going to beat my competitors on athleticism," she explained.

"For me, my strength is creativity. With that being one of the [judging] criteria, our thinking was, 'why don't we put all our eggs in that basket and really try and wow them? Maybe we can make a moment.'

"We never, ever expected the impact it might have."

The documentary reveals that head of the Australian Breaking Association, Lowe Napalan, only assisted Gunn's training "a handful" of times in the build-up to the Games, owing to the amount of administrative work taking up his time.

That meant that he only saw Gunn's controversial routine for the first time just before she performed at the Olympics.

"I was there side-stage," Napalan says in the film.

'I wouldn't let what happened take dancing away from me'

It was reported in November 2024 that the furore around her Olympic performance had led Gunn to quit breaking.

"I don't know where that came from," Gunn said.

"I wouldn't let what happened take dancing away from me. I love breaking, I'll always break, I'll always be a part of the community."

Her hope is that the release of the upcoming film can help shift the conversation.

"It feels nice to lay it all out there and now be able to look to the future. I'm actually excited about what's to come, which is the first time for a while," she said.

Details of organisations offering help and support with mental health are available at bbc.co.uk/actionline

articles.title: Ana Peleteiro y la congelación de óvulos de las futbolistas: una medida machista y peligrosa
articles.standfirst: Afirma que se puede condicionar la maternidad según la conveniencia del empleador
articles.summary: Afirma que se puede condicionar la maternidad según la conveniencia del empleador
articles.body: Ana Peleteiro es conocida por no callarse ante ninguna situación en la que opine que tiene algo que decir. En este caso lo ha hecho para comentar el anuncio hecho por la Federación Española de Fútbol en el sentido de que financiará el tratamiento para la congelación de óvulos de las futbolistas de la selección nacional y así puedan conciliar la maternidad con su carrera deportiva. Ana Peleteiro es madre y deportista de élite. En 2022, cuando ya era medallista olímpica y europea en triple salto, nació su primer hijo. Después ha sumado tres podios más, entre ellos oros europeos al aire libre e 'indoor'. La segunda ha nacido en este 2026. Y esta medida, y más su explicación como medio de 'conciliación' de las carreras deportivas y de la maternidad, no le parece precisamente positiva. En unas declaraciones difundidas a través de sus redes sociales, ha señalado que "una cosa es dar facilidades para ser madre y otra entrar en un sistema en el que lo más favorable para la institución es que no lo sea todavía" especificando que "se vende esta medida como feminista cuando en realidad es profundamente machista". Ana se pregunta "¿Por qué la institución para la que trabajan estas mujeres tiene interés en que retrasen su maternidad? ¿Pretende facilitar que las mujeres sean madres o pretende que no lo sean mientras están jugando?". La atleta señala que "si queremos hablar de conciliar deporte y maternidad hablemos de cosas como proteger los contratos durante el embarazo, garantizar la reincorporación, respetar los tiempos de recuperación y de posparto, facilitar el cuidado de los hijos y conseguir, en definitiva, que ser madre no penalice profesionalmente". Ana señala que "en vez de adaptar la competición a la maternidad se adaptan los tiempos reproductivos de las mujeres a la estructura", y señala que "aún hay algo que me preocupa más: Hoy, congelar óvulos es una opción, pero cuando esa opción te la ofrece la institución de la que depende tu carrera ¿En qué momento la opción puede empezar a convertirse en una expectativa?", es decir que sea exigible o esperable. "Una medida que aparentemente amplía la libertad de una mujer puede generar presión sobre una decisión que debería pertenecer exclusivamente a ella". "La pregunta no debería ser ¿Cómo conseguimos que una deportista retrase su maternidad? Sino ¿Cómo conseguimos que ser madre no penalice la carrera de una deportista?" Desde luego, Ana Peleteiro se expresa con claridad...

articles.title: A 16-year interlude: Shannon Rowbury’s wait for Olympic justice & her medal
articles.summary: More sports News: KOLKATA: For Shannon Rowbury, the 2012 London Olympics never really ended.The US middle-distance runner finished sixth in the women’s 1500m final that.
articles.body: KOLKATA: For Shannon Rowbury, the 2012 London Olympics never really ended.The US middle-distance runner finished sixth in the women’s 1500m final that night, believing she had missed out on an Olympic medal. But what followed over the next 13 years was the unravelling of one of the most tainted races in Olympic history.Turkey’s Asli Cakir Alptekin and Gamze Bulut, who finished first and second respectively, were later disqualified for doping. Russia’s Tatyana Tomashova, who was initially fourth and subsequently promoted to silver, was also disqualified following a doping case in 2024.As a result, Rowbury was eventually elevated to third. In June 2025, IOC officially reallocated the medals, making Rowbury the 2012 Olympic 1500m bronze medallist.Now, 16 years after the London race, the American will finally receive the medal physically at Los Angeles Olympics in 2028 — in front of the people who matter most to her.“I’m an optimistic person, so I always try to find the silver linings,” Rowbury said in Bhubaneswar last month. “It’s been a very difficult thing. When I found out the news, my entire body started shaking. I started sobbing. It was so much of the frustration I had carried within me about the unfairness of sport.”The London 1500m final has since become infamous, with six of the top nine finishers either disqualified or linked to performance-enhancing drug use. For Rowbury, however, the story is no longer simply about what she lost in London. It is about what clean sport ultimately gave her back.“I try to have gratitude for the fact that I do get justice in my story,” she said. “I will now have the opportunity to receive my medal in front of my two children. They will see their mother being recognised for winning with integrity, winning the right way.”That sense of justice has also shaped what Rowbury does today. She works with US Anti-Doping and speaks at conferences and events, trying to bring a human dimension to the fight against doping.Asked about India’s doping problem and what federations can do to bring down the numbers, Rowbury stressed that the answer cannot be limited to testing and punishment.“It’s not just about winning a race; it’s about sportsmanship and how you win,” she said, arguing for an ecosystem that encourages performance while making it clear that cheating carries consequences.“Once there is a clear directive that if you are cheating and you are caught, that you will miss your eligibility or there will be penalties, then hopefully that will disincentivise that performance.”But Rowbury also believes the solution needs to begin much earlier, during the development of young athletes and the creation of strong foundations built around the right values.Her own experience has also changed the way she looks at athletes — and perhaps explains why her transition into broadcasting has felt so natural.Rowbury began broadcasting while she was still competing, covering smaller meets in 2017 before retiring from competition in 2021. She has since worked in various roles with USA Track & Field, World Athletics and several broadcasters, and won an Emmy for her work during the Paris Olympics.For her, being an athlete first has given her a different perspective when she tells the stories of those still competing.That understanding has followed her to India, where she recently visited for the World Athletics Silver Level Continental Tour and worked on in-stadium commentary while also conducting a workshop for aspiring Indian broadcasters.But it is Los Angeles that now looms large in her mind. When Rowbury walks into an Olympic stadium in 2028, she will not be chasing another medal. Instead, she will finally receive the one she should have got 16 years ago.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Dancing With the Stars cast reveal: Savannah Bananas star Jackson Olson, Amber Glenn and Ezra Frech lead athletes on new season
articles.summary: The 35th season of DWTS begins on Tuesday, September 15.
articles.body:
It is time to finally return to the ballroom.

Season 35 of ABC's Dancing with the Stars is set to air on Tuesday, September 15, as part of a two-night premiere.

The show has become a fan favorite largely because of its cast mix of actors, athletes, and reality TV stars.

Ahead of Wednesday, only four cast members had been officially revealed. Summer House 's Ciara Miller, Love Island UK contestant Maura Higgins, Jimmy Kimmel Live 's Guillermo Rodriguez and the Savannah Bananas' Jackson Olson were the only cast members known.

The remainder of the cast was announced during Wednesday's episode of Good Morning America . Joining Olson are Ezra Frech and Amber Glenn as this season's athletes.

Olson, notably, was the first athlete revealed. Athletes tend to perform well on the show, but there have been varying degrees of success in recent seasons. Former NBA point guard Baron Davis was eliminated first last season, while Team USA rugby star Ilona Maher was the runner-up in 2024.

Olson, Frech and Glenn will look to be the first athlete to win the Mirrorball Trophy since former NBA player Iman Shumpert won alongside his pro Danielle Karagach in 2021.

So far, 12 athletes have won Dancing With the Stars .

Adam Rippon, 2018 - Former Olympic figure skater (this was an all-athlete season)

Rashad Jennings, 2017 - Former NFL running back

Laurie Hernandez, 2016 - Former Olympic gymnast

Meryl Davis, 2014 - Former Olympic ice dancer

Donald Driver, 2012 - Former NFL wide receiver

Hines Ward, 2011 - Former NFL wide receiver

Shawn Johnson, 2009 - Former Olympic gymnast

Kristi Yamaguchi, 2008 - Former Olympic figure skater

Helio Castroneves, Fall 2007 - IndyCar driver

Apolo Anton Ohno, Spring 2007 - Former Olympic speed skater

Emmitt Smith, 2006 - Former NFL running back

Olson is a member of the Savannah Bananas, best described as baseball's take on the Harlem Globetrotters. The games marry baseball with performance, and this merger is where Olson shines.

The second baseman doesn't have a background in music theater, but you could never tell from his performances on the field. He has orchestrated dances in honor of both The Greatest Showman and the musical Dear Evan Hansen , among several others.

Olson's ability to connect with the crowd carried over to his social media, where he has gone viral several times. As of Monday, August 31, his TikTok account has 2.2 million followers, while his Instagram has 1.1 million videos. He is already posting behind-the-scenes clips from DWTS on both platforms.

Glenn's name should sound familiar, as she helped Team USA take home the gold medal at the 2026 Olympics. An accomplished figure skater, Glenn has won the U.S. Championships three times — 2024, 2025 and 2026.

She one of the few women to land a triple axel in the history of the Winter Olympics.

Ezra Frech, Paralympic track and field athlete

Frech, who was born with congenital limb differences, is a two-time Paralympian. He competed at the 2020 Olympics and the 2024 Olympics. At the latter, he took home two gold medals, winning the 100m and the long jump.

Frech, who runs with a prosthetic on his left leg, has used his platform to be a philanthropist and a public speaker for those with physical disabilities.

articles.title: Jordan Chiles Has Michael Jordan Narrate LA Olympics 2028 Bid in Video, Flashes Custom Grills
articles.summary: United States gymnastics star Jordan Chiles has announced her bid for the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028 with the help of a legendary athlete.
articles.body:
United States gymnastics star Jordan Chiles has announced her bid for the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028 with the help of a legendary athlete.

Chiles posted a YouTube video announcing her return to the Olympics, and she had NBA icon Michael Jordan narrate it. Chiles also flashed a custom "LA 2028" grill at the end of the video.

49ers DE's Hilarious Plan for Australia Flight

Los Angeles 2028 will mark Chiles' third Olympics, and she'll hope to find even more success this time around.

She won a silver for team in 2020 and a gold for the same category in 2024, but she's still chasing some individual awards. As Jordan said in the video, "the dream is still there."

Who will join Chiles in Los Angeles remains to be seen, but U.S. star Simone Biles hasn't ruled out a return just yet. Regardless, the United States should be in the mix for gold, as it is at every Olympics, and Biles very well could take home a few individual gold medals.

articles.title: Jordan Chiles enlists Michael Jordan to announce her plan to make a run for 3rd Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028
articles.summary: Chiles made the announcement a day after UCLA announced that she was returning to its gymnastics program as a coach.
articles.body:
Jordan Chiles is planning to run it back.

The two-time Olympic medal-winning gymnast announced Wednesday that she's preparing to compete in the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.

Chiles had previously been mum about her plans. She hasn't competed internationally since she helped lead USA to team gold at the Paris Olympics in 2024. When asked about her 2028 plans, she told NBC Sports in August that "the wait is still on."

That wait — for a decision at least — is now over. And it adds up that Chiles would want to compete again on the Olympic stage in Los Angeles.

A Los Angeles resident who graduated from UCLA in June , Chiles won four NCAA championships (two on bars, two on floor) while competing for the Bruins. On Tuesday, UCLA announced that Chiles would return to the gymnastics program for the 2027 season as a student coach.

A day later, Chiles announced her intention for the 2028 Olympics. That news wasn't announced via a UCLA press release. Chiles, instead, enlisted a little help.

She made the announcement via an Instagram video narrated by her namesake, Michael Jordan. She captioned the video: "LA 2028… WHY NOT?"

Chiles, of course, isn't guaranteed a spot on the 2028 roster. She'll have to earn her spot, like always. The U.S. Olympic team is selected via a combination of trials and a selection committee.

But she'll certainly have a leg up on making the team. Chiles helped lead USA to team silver in Tokyo in 2021 and team gold in Paris in 2024. She was also awarded the individual bronze medal in the floor competition in Paris. That medal was contested over a score adjustment and it remains in dispute more than two years later.

Regardless of the status of that bronze medal, Chiles is a decorated and competition-tested Olympic veteran.

Chiles is the fourth member of the 2024 U.S. Olympic team known to be interested in competing in Los Angeles. Hezly Rivera, Jade Carey and Suni Lee are all believed to be targeting a return to the Olympics in 2028.

As for seven-time Olympic gold medalist Simone Biles, her decision awaits. Biles told CNN in April that she's "still at 50-50" on whether she intends to make a run at the 2028 Games.

articles.title: Tara Davis-Woodhall 'lucky to be alive' after car crash
articles.summary: Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall says she is "lucky and blessed to be alive" after being involved in a car crash.
articles.body:
Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall says she is "lucky and blessed to be alive" after being involved in a car crash.

The 27-year-old American was on her way to training last week when she was involved in a "very scary" head-on collision, leaving her with a "severe" concussion.

While not ruling herself out of this month's inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest, the reigning world champion says she has been unable to train since the accident.

"Luckily I walked away without any major injuries," Davis-Woodhall wrote on social media.

"At this point I'm working with my team and doctors to get healthy, but I'm not sure if I will be ready to compete at Ultimate Championships next week. More updates to come."

Davis-Woodhall said her injuries were not life-threatening but that both cars, which were going at about 20mph, were written off.

"It's really unfortunate timing; I am at the peak of my training right now," she said.

"I'm as fast as I've ever been. I'm as strong as I've ever been. So this decision is very difficult for me. I don't know where I am right now."

The championships in Hungary start on 11 September, where athletes will compete for a top prize of £111,000.

The competition brings together Olympic, world and Diamond League champions, as well as the year's leading performers in a three-day end-of-season event.

Davis-Woodhall won long jump gold at the 2024 Olympics in Paris, before winning the Worlds in Tokyo a year later.

articles.summary: Gymnast Jordan Chiles will attempt a return to the Olympics in 2028 in Los Angeles, the gold medalist from the Paris Games announced Wednesday — with an assist from Michael Jordan.
articles.body: Gymnast Jordan Chiles will attempt a return to the Olympics in 2028 in Los Angeles, the gold medalist from the Paris Games announced Wednesday — with an assist from Michael Jordan. Jordan lent his voice as the narrator for Chiles’ announcement video on Instagram, in which she posted “LA 2028… WHY NOT?” The video features overhead shots of the Southern California coastline and Chiles at a beach. “Why again? Because the dream is still there,” Jordan narrates. “Why continue? Because there’s still more to give.” Chiles, 25, is named after the NBA legend and is no stranger to Los Angeles, attending UCLA and competing for the Bruins’ gymnastics team, with whom she’s a four-time NCAA champion. She also won the team gold medal with the U.S. at the 2024 Paris Games. She infamously had an individual bronze medal at the competition stripped following a controversial ruling, which she’s still appealing. Chiles was part of America’s silver-winning team at the Tokyo Games in 2020. She turned heads at that competition when she stepped in for Simone Biles, who withdrew before the finals to focus on her mental health. “When the world asks why she’s back for a third time, the answer’s simple,” Jordan says in Wednesday’s video. “Why not?” Chiles replies.

articles.title: Official: Landon Emenalo, Shim Mheuka, Kiano Dyer complete late loan moves
articles.summary: Just in time
articles.body:
The transfer window slammed shut last night, but there are always a few late deals that only get announced the following morning. Unfortunately, a new midfielder is not one of those despite some speculation today about veteran free agent Georginio Wijnaldum.

The three confirmed moves are loans for Academy standouts Landon Emenalo, 18, Shim Mheuka, 18, and Kiano Dyer, 19 — the two 18-year-olds both going to Celtic in Scotland and Dyer joining League Two side Chesterfield FC. Dyer and Mheuka already have at least one senior appearance to their name while Emenalo (son of our former sporting director Michael Emenalo) was with the first-team on our preseason tour this summer and caught the eye of many observers.

It's certainly a bold move for both Emenalo and Mheuka to be joining the Scottish champions, where they will be competing for minutes against seasoned internationals like former Arsenal left back Kieran Tierney or Denmark striker Kasper Høgh. Celtic manager Martin O'Neill spoke highly of the two teenagers upon their arrival, but we'll just have to wait and see how that translates to minutes at the top level.

"Landon is a very good player we have followed for some time, he will give us some real quality. He has many attributes which I think can benefit us, he is very quick and athletic but also very composed on the ball and while he can defend he certainly gets up the pitch into attacking positions too. I know he has a real desire to do well for us and I am sure he will, as he adds strong competition and support on our left side." "Shim has great quality, hence Chelsea extending his contract, however I think this period of his career, spent with us, will be beneficial to him and obviously to us. I look forward to working with him, he is a player who I think can give us another great attacking dimension and I'm sure he will make an important contribution to Celtic." -Martin O'Neill; sources: Celtic FC ; Celtic FC
